name: Coq Au Vin (Chicken Braised in Red Wine)
headnote: Daniel Gritzer explains that the dish was built around an old rooster that needed hours of cooking, and that using a modern tender hen the same way just dries out the breast, which he demonstrates with a side-by-side of 20-minute and 45-minute breast meat. His fix is to brown all the chicken, braise only the legs for about an hour, and add the breasts for the last 20 minutes, with a short wine marinade beforehand so the quick-cooking breast still tastes like part of the braise. He tested marinating times and found even 25 minutes, the time it takes to prep everything else, gives most of the benefit, and he argues the specific wine barely matters once stock, pork, mushrooms and aromatics are in the pot. For the sauce he rejects beurre manie in favor of reducing a gelatin-rich stock and finishing with butter, warning that heavy reduction concentrates salt so seasoning should wait until the end.
comment_digest: The most substantive criticism concerns the sauce. One detailed reviewer argues the 1:1 wine-to-stock ratio yields too little wine flavor and too pale a sauce, preferring roughly 3:1 or no stock at all, and reports that even with two packets of gelatin and hard reducing it lacked body until thickened with a cornstarch slurry. A second cook also reached for cornstarch, partly because the article says to pour off most of the fat after browning while the recipe steps omit that, leaving the dish too fatty to finish with butter. Against that, another says reducing by two-thirds gave a glossy sauce needing no thickener, so patience may be the variable. Scaling matters: using one 4-pound chicken instead of two small ones leaves too much liquid unless the wine and stock are cut too. Carrots are contested. Two readers raise food-safety unease about the partly cooked breasts resting at room temperature.
flags: The published recipe steps do not include the article's instruction to pour off excess fat after browning the chicken - two reviewers were tripped up by this. Some comments end in 'Read More' and may be cut off.
